screens.title: What is DataStax Enterprise?
screens.narratorSegment: DataStax Enterprise is a commercial distribution of Apache Cassandra that bundles integrated engines and enterprise features to support a wider range of data workloads. At its core DSE retains Cassandra's high-availability, distributed storage model while adding Search through Solr, a native Graph layer, Spark-based Analytics, and advanced security. This means you can index text, traverse relationships, and run analytics directly on your operational dataset without exporting it. A useful mental model is thinking of DSE as Cassandra with purpose-built toolkits for text search, graph traversals, and analytics that run against the same storage. For example, an application can index product descriptions for keyword search while the same rows are available to Spark for nightly batch feature extraction. A common misconception is thinking DSE replaces Cassandra; instead it extends it and keeps Cassandra's storage and replication behavior unchanged. Why this matters in practice: integrated engines cut data movement and reduce synchronization errors between systems. When you design systems with DSE, prioritize understanding which engine serves which query pattern so you avoid overloading a single node with conflicting workloads. screens.title: DSE Search: CQL index and queries
screens.narratorSegment: DSE Search integrates Apache Solr into Cassandra so you can index text and run full-text and faceted searches directly against table columns. The key step is creating a custom index that uses the Solr secondary index implementation; that index maps chosen columns to a Solr schema and provides the solr_query entry point in CQL. The chapter includes a full example that creates a keyspace, a table named articles, and a custom index that indexes title and content fields. In practice, you would enable DSE Search on your cluster and then create the index with WITH OPTIONS specifying schema and field types. After inserting rows, you use SELECT with a solr_query payload to find documents that match a term, for example searching for the word "cassandra" or combining text queries with filter queries for structured filtering. A common error is indexing too many large text fields without considering index storage and update cost; plan which columns truly need full-text capabilities. Reading the CQL example will show how Solr-specific options are passed via WITH OPTIONS and how the solr_query JSON lets you combine keyword search and filters. Practice reading and identifying the indexed fields and query patterns to gain practical fluency.

keyIdea.title: Search pattern
keyIdea.text: Create a Solr-backed custom index and query it using the solr_query field in CQL to combine full-text and filtered search.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › DSE Search: CQL
Index example (conceptual)
This CQL shows the pattern for creating a Solr-backed custom index and issuing a search query using solr_query.
CREATE KEYSPACE IF NOT EXISTS myapp WITH replication = {'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'datacenter1': 3};
USE myapp;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS articles (
    article_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    content TEXT,
    author TEXT,
    publish_date TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE CUSTOM INDEX articles_search_idx ON articles (title, content) USING 'com.datastax.bdp.search.solr.Cql3SolrSecondaryIndex'
WITH OPTIONS = {
    'schema_name': 'articles_schema',
    'solr_query_field': 'solr_query',
    'default_text_field': 'content',
    'fields': {
        'title': { 'type': 'text_general', 'indexed': true, 'stored': true },
        'content': { 'type': 'text_general', 'indexed': true, 'stored': true },
        'author': { 'type': 'string', 'indexed': true, 'stored': true }
    }
};

SELECT * FROM articles WHERE solr_query = '{ "q": "cassandra" }';
SELECT * FROM articles WHERE solr_query = '{ "q": "search capabilities", "fq": "author:Bob" }';
Note how the WITH OPTIONS block passes Solr schema and fields. The solr_query JSON payload runs the search from CQL. Avoid indexing unnecessary large fields to keep index size reasonable.
Explanation
  • CREATE CUSTOM INDEX ties a Solr index to specified columns so text can be searched.
  • The solr_query field accepts a Solr JSON string that can include queries and filter queries.
  • WITH OPTIONS configures field types and the default text field used for free-text queries.
Concrete example
Indexing product descriptions so users can search with keywords and then filter results by category or price using filter queries.
Common mistake
Indexing too many or very large text columns without planning index storage and update costs can slow writes and grow disk usage quickly.

screens.title: Configure and Query a DSE Search Index (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: Working with DSE Search generally follows a clear sequence of steps that connect cluster configuration, schema design, indexing, and queries. First, ensure your DSE cluster has search enabled; in practice you start DSE with search flags and confirm node settings. Next, you design a keyspace and table that model your operational data, then decide which columns require full-text indexing. After that, create a CREATE CUSTOM INDEX statement that maps chosen columns to a Solr schema and set options like default_text_field and field types. Insert or update rows in the table; DSE maintains the Solr index as data changes. Finally, query using the solr_query field in CQL, combining free-text queries with filter queries for structured constraints. The chapter's hands-on activity outlines these conceptual steps. A practical tip: begin by indexing a small set of fields and monitor index size, query latency, and write throughput. A common pitfall is assuming instant parity between writes and index availability; plan for index commit behavior and test with representative loads. This workflow helps you reason about operational trade-offs and where to focus monitoring and tuning when you enable search on a production cluster.

Start DSE with search enabled and verify node configuration. This prepares nodes to host Solr cores.

Model your data in Cassandra tables and choose columns that require full-text indexing.

screens.title: DSE Graph: Model and use cases
screens.narratorSegment: DSE Graph is a native graph layer built on top of Cassandra that uses Apache TinkerPop and the Gremlin traversal language for modeling and querying connected data. In contrast to table lookups, graph databases represent entities as nodes and relationships as edges, making multi-hop traversals efficient for queries that depend on relationships. Use cases include social networks, recommendation engines, master data management, and fraud detection — where understanding chains of connections is essential. For example, fraud detection often requires traversing from a payment to linked accounts, devices, and transactions to find anomalous patterns. Gremlin expresses traversals like "find friends of friends who live in New York" as a sequence of steps rather than large joins. A common misconception is that graphs always replace tables; instead graphs complement tables when relationship queries dominate. When modeling, capture the relationships you need to traverse and avoid modeling every attribute as an edge. In practice, start with a small graph model for critical traversals, test query latency at scale, and use graph analytics where multi-hop patterns reveal insights that would be very expensive with table joins. What relationship queries in your domain would benefit most from graph traversals?

What DSE Graph provides
A native graph database on Cassandra using TinkerPop and Gremlin for traversals and modeling connected data efficiently.
Use cases
  • Social networks and recommendation filters where relationships drive results.
  • Fraud detection that analyzes chains of linked accounts and devices.
  • Master data management where relationships between entities must be tracked.
Model example
Nodes: user, device, account. Edges: owns, logs-in-from, transacts-with. Query traversals can follow edges to identify suspicious chains.

Find friends of friends in a social graph and filter by location to produce local recommendations or to detect clusters of suspicious connections.

screens.title: DSE Analytics: Spark integrated with Cassandra
screens.narratorSegment: DSE Analytics integrates Apache Spark with Cassandra so teams can run real-time and batch analytics on operational data without moving it to a separate data warehouse. Spark jobs can use Spark S Q L, streaming, and machine learning libraries to process rows stored in Cassandra. The key advantage is reduced operational complexity: rather than creating ETL pipelines to copy data, you can run analytics in place and keep data consistent. Common analytics workloads include real-time dashboards, anomaly detection, and training models for recommendations. In an architecture view, Cassandra remains the storage layer, and Spark executors run on the cluster to read and process data with low latency. A practical tip is to plan for resource isolation: Spark executors and Cassandra reads compete for C P U, memory, and network, so size the cluster and tune executor settings carefully. Misunderstanding resource needs is a frequent source of performance issues. When designing analytics on DSE, test representative streaming and batch workloads, measure input and output and latency, and iterate on executor memory and partitioning strategy. The goal is to get analytics insight quickly while preserving the operational performance your applications depend on.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › DSE Analytics
What it is
Spark integrated into DSE so you can run analytics jobs directly against Cassandra-stored data for both batch and streaming use cases.
Common workloads
  • Real-time dashboards that aggregate operational metrics.
  • Anomaly detection and streaming alerts.
  • Machine learning training on recent production data.
Architecture note
Cassandra remains the storage layer. Spark reads data and runs processing in-place. This avoids ETL but introduces resource sharing trade-offs.
Practical tip

A streaming pipeline that consumes events, writes them to Cassandra, and runs Spark Streaming jobs to update a real-time dashboard with rolling aggregates and anomaly scores.

screens.title: Integrated DSE Engines vs Separate Stacks
screens.narratorSegment: One powerful selling point of DSE is that it allows you to run search, graph, and analytics without operating multiple independent clusters. However, it's important to weigh trade-offs. Integrated engines reduce operational overhead and eliminate ETL, which lowers latency between operational writes and analytical or search results. On the other hand, integrating multiple engines on shared nodes means resources are shared: Solr cores use C P U and disk, Spark executors use memory and network, and graph traversals can drive random access patterns. The chapter cautions against underestimating configuration complexity and resource planning. A practical approach is to test representative workloads early and consider dedicating nodes for heavy analytics jobs or tuning compaction and indexing schedules. Another common mistake is over-indexing; indexing everything because you can will quickly increase disk usage and index maintenance overhead. Compare the decision with your use case: if you need tight consistency across workloads and lower operational complexity, integrated DSE is a strong choice. If extreme isolation for heavy analytics or search is required, separate clusters might be justified. The right choice depends on workload patterns, resource budgets, and operational capacity.

keyIdea.text: Integrated engines simplify operations and remove ETL, but require careful resource planning to prevent contention and performance issues.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Integrated vs Separate
Integrated DSE
  • Single platform: Cassandra storage + search, graph, analytics engines.
  • Reduces data movement and simplifies consistency across workloads.
  • Lower operational overhead when workloads are moderate and balanced.
Separate Stacks
  • Isolate heavy workloads to dedicated clusters for predictable performance.
  • More operational complexity due to maintaining ETL and synchronization.
  • May be appropriate for extreme scale or strict isolation requirements.
Decision checklist
Workload pattern
Are queries balanced between operational reads, search, and analytics?
Resource needs
Will Spark or Solr require dedicated CPU/memory beyond a shared cluster's capacity?
Operational capacity
Can your team manage multiple clusters or prefer a single integrated platform?

screens.title: DSE Advanced Security
screens.narratorSegment: DSE Advanced Security strengthens Cassandra's native controls with features designed for enterprise compliance and protection of sensitive data. Key capabilities include role-based access control, encryption at rest and in transit, auditing, and integration with external authentication systems like LDAP and Kerberos. Role-based access control lets you assign roles to users and grant permissions at multiple granularity levels; DSE can even enforce column-level permissions, which is useful when you must ensure only authorized roles can view particular sensitive fields. Encryption reduces risk by protecting data on disk and over the network. Auditing records access events so you can investigate who performed what action. Integrating with external authentication systems allows centralized identity management and alignment with corporate policies. A common mistake is assuming default Cassandra authentication alone is sufficient for regulated environments: DSE adds features designed specifically for compliance. When planning security, identify sensitive columns, establish least-privilege roles, and balance audit verbosity against performance and storage costs. These controls help you meet regulatory requirements while enabling secure access to data-driven applications. DSE Advanced Security means dse provides rbac, encryption, auditing, and external auth integrations to meet enterprise compliance and protect sensitive data.. screens.title: Planning cluster topology and resources
screens.narratorSegment: When enabling DSE components you must plan cluster topology and resource allocation carefully to avoid unexpected bottlenecks. Each engine has different resource patterns: DSE Search manages Solr cores and disk for indexes; DSE Analytics runs Spark executors that need memory and C P U; DSE Graph can create random access patterns that increase read amplification. A practical planning approach begins with mapping workloads: estimate write throughput, search query rates, traversal complexity, and analytics job frequency. Next, prototype with representative data and workloads to observe C P U, memory, disk, and network usage. Consider dedicating node tiers if one workload dominates — for example, reserve nodes for heavy Spark jobs or run mixed workloads with tuned executor and core settings. Monitor index growth, compaction behavior, and query latency; these metrics reveal when to increase disk or split responsibilities across nodes. A common mistake is underestimating index maintenance during heavy writes. Another is not testing multi-engine interactions under realistic traffic. Use gradual rollouts and capacity-testing to find safe defaults. The outcome is a topology and resource plan that balances performance, cost, and operational complexity for your specific application needs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what DataStax Enterprise adds to Apache Cassandra and why those additions matter in real systems. DataStax Enterprise, or DSE, is a commercial distribution of Cassandra that bundles specialized engines — search powered by Solr, a native graph layer using TinkerPop and Gremlin, integrated analytics with Spark, and advanced security features. Together these engines let you use one unified data platform instead of stitching separate systems together. That reduces operational complexity and avoids repeated extract-transform-load steps that waste time and can introduce inconsistency. For example, an e-commerce catalog can store product rows in Cassandra, index text fields with DSE Search for fast keyword and faceted queries, and use DSE Analytics to run daily recommendations without copying data to a separate analytics cluster. A common misconception is that DSE replaces Cassandra; in fact it extends Cassandra with engines that run on the same data nodes. Over the upcoming screens we will examine DSE Search, DSE Graph, DSE Analytics, and the advanced security controls, show a simple CQL example of search indexing and queries, and discuss planning and common configuration pitfalls. By the end you will be able to explain which DSE feature fits common use cases and why integrated engines simplify architectures.

These learning objectives focus your work with DataStax Enterprise so you can both explain features and carry out basic configuration tasks. First, you'll explain the core DSE components and why combining search, graph, analytics, and security in one product reduces complexity for many applications. A concrete example is running product search and analytics against the same operational dataset. Second, you'll describe specific use cases for DSE Search, DSE Graph, and DSE Analytics; for instance, search for text and facets in catalogs, graph traversals for social or fraud detection, and Spark jobs for real-time dashboards. Third, you will follow the conceptual steps to configure and interact with a simple DSE Search index, including creating a keyspace, table, and a custom Solr-backed index. Finally, you'll understand the advanced security features DSE offers, including role-based access control and encryption, and why they matter for compliance. Each objective combines a skill with a practical reason to master it. Keep these goals visible as you move through the lesson examples and configuration steps.

This second objectives slide makes the goals actionable and practical. You will practice interpreting example CQL for creating Solr-backed indexes and run conceptual queries that use the solr_query field. That means you should be able to read a CREATE CUSTOM INDEX statement and identify which columns are indexed and which Solr options affect text analysis. You will also learn to choose between graph traversals and search queries by comparing problem patterns: use graph traversal when relationships and multi-hop queries matter; use search when free text and filtering are the priority. Another objective is to reason about capacity and topology. When enabling search, graph, or analytics on the same cluster, resource planning is essential: index storage, search cores, Spark executor memory, and network input and output all influence node sizing. Finally, you'll be able to explain common misconfigurations that lead to bottlenecks and how to approach validating a DSE deployment. These objectives prepare you to move from reading documentation to making thoughtful design and configuration choices.

DataStax Enterprise is a commercial distribution of Apache Cassandra that bundles integrated engines and enterprise features to support a wider range of data workloads. At its core DSE retains Cassandra's high-availability, distributed storage model while adding Search through Solr, a native Graph layer, Spark-based Analytics, and advanced security. This means you can index text, traverse relationships, and run analytics directly on your operational dataset without exporting it. A useful mental model is thinking of DSE as Cassandra with purpose-built toolkits for text search, graph traversals, and analytics that run against the same storage. For example, an application can index product descriptions for keyword search while the same rows are available to Spark for nightly batch feature extraction. A common misconception is thinking DSE replaces Cassandra; instead it extends it and keeps Cassandra's storage and replication behavior unchanged. Why this matters in practice: integrated engines cut data movement and reduce synchronization errors between systems. When you design systems with DSE, prioritize understanding which engine serves which query pattern so you avoid overloading a single node with conflicting workloads. What question will you ask first when evaluating whether DSE fits your architecture?

DSE Search integrates Apache Solr into Cassandra so you can index text and run full-text and faceted searches directly against table columns. The key step is creating a custom index that uses the Solr secondary index implementation; that index maps chosen columns to a Solr schema and provides the solr_query entry point in CQL. The chapter includes a full example that creates a keyspace, a table named articles, and a custom index that indexes title and content fields. In practice, you would enable DSE Search on your cluster and then create the index with WITH OPTIONS specifying schema and field types. After inserting rows, you use SELECT with a solr_query payload to find documents that match a term, for example searching for the word "cassandra" or combining text queries with filter queries for structured filtering. A common error is indexing too many large text fields without considering index storage and update cost; plan which columns truly need full-text capabilities. Reading the CQL example will show how Solr-specific options are passed via WITH OPTIONS and how the solr_query JSON lets you combine keyword search and filters. Practice reading and identifying the indexed fields and query patterns to gain practical fluency.

Working with DSE Search generally follows a clear sequence of steps that connect cluster configuration, schema design, indexing, and queries. First, ensure your DSE cluster has search enabled; in practice you start DSE with search flags and confirm node settings. Next, you design a keyspace and table that model your operational data, then decide which columns require full-text indexing. After that, create a CREATE CUSTOM INDEX statement that maps chosen columns to a Solr schema and set options like default_text_field and field types. Insert or update rows in the table; DSE maintains the Solr index as data changes. Finally, query using the solr_query field in CQL, combining free-text queries with filter queries for structured constraints. The chapter's hands-on activity outlines these conceptual steps. A practical tip: begin by indexing a small set of fields and monitor index size, query latency, and write throughput. A common pitfall is assuming instant parity between writes and index availability; plan for index commit behavior and test with representative loads. This workflow helps you reason about operational trade-offs and where to focus monitoring and tuning when you enable search on a production cluster.

DSE Graph is a native graph layer built on top of Cassandra that uses Apache TinkerPop and the Gremlin traversal language for modeling and querying connected data. In contrast to table lookups, graph databases represent entities as nodes and relationships as edges, making multi-hop traversals efficient for queries that depend on relationships. Use cases include social networks, recommendation engines, master data management, and fraud detection — where understanding chains of connections is essential. For example, fraud detection often requires traversing from a payment to linked accounts, devices, and transactions to find anomalous patterns. Gremlin expresses traversals like "find friends of friends who live in New York" as a sequence of steps rather than large joins. A common misconception is that graphs always replace tables; instead graphs complement tables when relationship queries dominate. When modeling, capture the relationships you need to traverse and avoid modeling every attribute as an edge. In practice, start with a small graph model for critical traversals, test query latency at scale, and use graph analytics where multi-hop patterns reveal insights that would be very expensive with table joins. What relationship queries in your domain would benefit most from graph traversals?

DSE Analytics integrates Apache Spark with Cassandra so teams can run real-time and batch analytics on operational data without moving it to a separate data warehouse. Spark jobs can use Spark S Q L, streaming, and machine learning libraries to process rows stored in Cassandra. The key advantage is reduced operational complexity: rather than creating ETL pipelines to copy data, you can run analytics in place and keep data consistent. Common analytics workloads include real-time dashboards, anomaly detection, and training models for recommendations. In an architecture view, Cassandra remains the storage layer, and Spark executors run on the cluster to read and process data with low latency. A practical tip is to plan for resource isolation: Spark executors and Cassandra reads compete for C P U, memory, and network, so size the cluster and tune executor settings carefully. Misunderstanding resource needs is a frequent source of performance issues. When designing analytics on DSE, test representative streaming and batch workloads, measure input and output and latency, and iterate on executor memory and partitioning strategy. The goal is to get analytics insight quickly while preserving the operational performance your applications depend on.

One powerful selling point of DSE is that it allows you to run search, graph, and analytics without operating multiple independent clusters. However, it's important to weigh trade-offs. Integrated engines reduce operational overhead and eliminate ETL, which lowers latency between operational writes and analytical or search results. On the other hand, integrating multiple engines on shared nodes means resources are shared: Solr cores use C P U and disk, Spark executors use memory and network, and graph traversals can drive random access patterns. The chapter cautions against underestimating configuration complexity and resource planning. A practical approach is to test representative workloads early and consider dedicating nodes for heavy analytics jobs or tuning compaction and indexing schedules. Another common mistake is over-indexing; indexing everything because you can will quickly increase disk usage and index maintenance overhead. Compare the decision with your use case: if you need tight consistency across workloads and lower operational complexity, integrated DSE is a strong choice. If extreme isolation for heavy analytics or search is required, separate clusters might be justified. The right choice depends on workload patterns, resource budgets, and operational capacity.

When planning security, identify sensitive columns, establish least-privilege roles, and balance audit verbosity against performance and storage costs. These controls help you meet regulatory requirements while enabling secure access to data-driven applications.
